p: Elena gave Priya the Copilot rollout and a quarter to get every engineer on it.
Priya chose Copilot Business, moved the people on personal plans onto company seats, and turned it on in waves, so Ken could fence off the patient adjacent code first.
Anders asked Copilot to explain a module he wrote, caught it getting one thing backwards, and called it a decent junior he has to check.
Elena wanted a target for each engineer's acceptance rate. Priya talked her into measuring team results instead.
Then, at 2:14 on Sunday night, Tomasz wrote from Kraków. His team had assigned an issue to Copilot, waited in their editors, and nothing happened.
Tomasz Nowak. Runs engineering in Kraków. His people sign up first for everything new.
Anders Lindqvist. Priya's old mentor, now trying Copilot on his own Terraform.
Devin Marsh. Engineer. Always looking for the setting that makes it faster.
Renata Vega. Junior engineer, a few weeks in. She asks what everyone else won't.
Ken Ito. Security lead. His exclusions keep Copilot out of patient adjacent code.
Joyce Cho. The CTO, and the rollout's sponsor. She likes a chart.
Chapter two. Two Kinds of Agent.

She didn't sleep after that. At 2:40 she gave up, made tea, and sat at the kitchen table with her laptop and the GitHub docs, reading the way she used to read for exams, with a pen in her hand even though there was nothing to write on.

By five she had the answer, and it was embarrassing in the useful way. Copilot had two things that people called an agent. One lived inside your editor and worked while you watched. The other lived on GitHub, and once you handed it an issue it went off and did the work somewhere else, on its own, and came back with a pull request. Kraków had used the second one and waited for the first.

She typed a reply to Tomasz and deleted it, because a paragraph at five in the morning wasn't going to fix it. Can I join your 3 PM? I'll show you where it went. I didn't know either until an hour ago.
His answer came back in under a minute. Kraków was eight hours ahead, and he'd been at his desk since nine their time. Yes. Bring coffee for yourself. We already had ours.

At 6:30 her phone buzzed with five new photos of index cards, purple felt tip on lined white. Asha had been up too. Thirty years of nights did that to a person, and retirement hadn't undone it. Across the top card she'd written: Week three. You don't need to know everything. You need to know who's on your shift.
Under it, smaller, a second line. And who's on the next one.
Asha's Shift Notes: two kinds of agent.
Asha's first card was about staffing. Some help works beside you. Some help works the next shift while you sleep. Don't confuse them, and don't manage them the same way.

Under it Priya wrote what the docs said. Agent mode is a mode of Copilot Chat in your editor. You give it a task in plain words. It decides which files to open, makes edits across several of them, proposes terminal commands, reads the output and the errors, and tries again until the task is done or it needs you. You're there the whole time. You see each edit, keep it or undo it, and approve the commands it wants to run. In VS Code, common read only commands run without asking by default, and anything risky waits for you. It's synchronous: it works while you watch.

The Copilot coding agent works on GitHub. You assign it an issue the way you'd assign a teammate, or start it from chat or from the agents page on GitHub.com. It works on its own, in a development environment that GitHub Actions provides, pushes its commits to a new branch, and opens a draft pull request. When it's done it asks you for a review. It's asynchronous: it works while you're doing something else. GitHub renamed it Copilot cloud agent in 2026, and the current docs use that name. Older material, and possibly the exam, still say coding agent, so learn both names. On Copilot Business and Enterprise, an administrator has to turn on the coding agent policy before anyone can use it, and can choose which repositories it works in.

How the exam asks it. If the scenario says "in the IDE" or "while the developer watches," it's agent mode. If it says "assigned an issue," "works in the background," or "opens a pull request," it's the coding agent.
The second card was the one Priya taped to her monitor. Night shift hands off. Day shift takes report and checks the patient. Nobody takes report and goes home.

The coding agent's pull request is its report. The pull request links to a session log, where you can see what it tried, what it ran, and why it changed what it changed. If you want something different, you leave a comment on the pull request that mentions @copilot, and it picks the work back up and pushes new commits.

GitHub builds the review into the design. The coding agent can push to only one branch: a new branch whose name starts with copilot/, or, when you mention @copilot on an existing pull request, that pull request's branch. It can't mark its pull request ready for review, and it can't approve or merge it. The developer who asked it for the work can't be the one who approves it, so someone else has to review it. By default, GitHub Actions workflows don't run on its pull request until someone with write access approves them, because the code came from an agent and nobody has read it yet. A repository can choose to let them run automatically. Its environment has a firewall that limits internet access by default. If it needs tools or dependencies to build and test your project, you preinstall them with a workflow file named .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml. Its work uses GitHub Actions minutes as well as your plan's usage allowance. It does best with a well scoped issue: a clear description, acceptance criteria, and pointers to the files that matter.

How the exam asks it. Know the guardrails: one branch only (a new copilot/ branch, or the pull request's branch when you mention @copilot on it), no approving or merging its own work, the requester can't approve, workflows wait for approval by default, and you ask for changes by mentioning @copilot in a comment.

The third card was the only one in Asha's handwriting that looked rushed, as if she'd written it fast so she couldn't talk herself out of it. My first year. I was twenty nine, and the off going nurse was someone I wanted to be. She said the count was right, and I signed without counting. It was off by one vial. Three of us spent until four in the morning finding it in the wrong drawer. A signature means you checked. That's all it means.

Agent mode asks before it runs a terminal command that isn't on an approved list. That click is your signature. In VS Code, common read only commands are approved by default and risky ones like rm still ask. You can approve a command once, for the session or workspace, or always, add your own rules in settings, or pick a permission level like Allow all that skips the prompts. Some teams extend automatic approval to harmless commands such as running tests or listing files. Anything that changes state, like deploying, deleting, migrating a database, or applying infrastructure, needs a person who reads the command first. When you aren't sure what a command does, deny it and ask Copilot to explain it. Agent mode also keeps checkpoints in VS Code, so you can roll the files back to an earlier point in the conversation, but a checkpoint can't undo what a command already did to a server.
How the exam asks it. The responsible answer validates before acting: read the proposed command, prefer a dry run or plan, and keep human approval for anything that changes state.
The fourth card was a list. Small job, small team. Long shift, clean handoff. Send a runner instead of leaving the bedside.

Copilot Edits is how you make changes across several files from one conversation. When you already know which files are involved, you add them yourself and Copilot proposes changes only there, and you review each one before you keep it. Agent mode finds the files on its own, which is better when you don't know where the change goes. One status note. VS Code deprecated its built in Edit mode in June 2026 and points people to agent mode, or to a custom agent that behaves like Edit mode. The exam outline still names Copilot Edits, so learn what it's for: you pick the files and Copilot proposes changes only there.

Every chat session has a limited context window, and the conversation history is part of what fills it. In a long session, early decisions get crowded out and the answers drift. The fix is to start a new session for each new task, with a short summary of the decisions that still matter. Newer editors also let the main agent hand a focused job, like searching the codebase or reading a long log, to a subagent. The subagent works in its own context and hands back only the result, so the main session stays clean. Your editor keeps a list of sessions, and in VS Code you can hand a session off to the coding agent to finish on GitHub. Exact menus change between releases, so learn what each one is for.
How the exam asks it. Long, drifting sessions point to context. The answer is a fresh session, a tighter prompt, or a subagent, not repeating yourself louder.
The last card had a door drawn on it. Every new tool on the cart is a new way in. Know who brought it and what it can reach.

The Model Context Protocol, MCP, is an open standard for connecting AI agents to outside tools and data. An MCP server might let agent mode query a database, read a ticket system, or drive a browser. In VS Code you configure servers for a project in .vscode/mcp.json. For the coding agent, a repository administrator adds them in the repository's Copilot settings, and the GitHub MCP server comes set up with access limited to that repository. On Business and Enterprise an organization policy controls whether members can use MCP servers at all. Use servers you trust, give them the narrowest access that works, and remember that a server's tools act with whatever credentials you hand it.

Priya added one more line on Wednesday, after Ken asked. Content exclusions don't reach everywhere. When she checked in October, GitHub's docs said exclusions weren't supported in agent mode in VS Code, that the coding agent had only started honoring them in a public preview, and that third party agents weren't covered. Exclusions also miss symlinks, remote filesystems, and type or symbol information the editor passes along indirectly. That list changes, so read the current one before you count on an exclusion inside agent mode or the coding agent.
How the exam asks it. MCP extends what an agent can reach. The safe answers vet the server, limit its access, and respect the organization's MCP policy.

At seven she was on video with Kraków, a cup of coffee she didn't want in her hand. Tomasz sat at the head of a table with four of his engineers. Behind them the window was full of a gray October afternoon.
We assigned the logging issue to Copilot at ten this morning. Then we opened our editors and waited for it to start. Nothing happened. So, is it broken, or are we?
Nobody at the table was smiling. They had been the first team to sign up for anything new for two years, and Priya could see they were bracing to be the team that got it wrong.
Kraków assigned an issue to Copilot this morning, and nothing seems to be happening. What should Priya tell them?
Answer. Tell them the agent's queue runs slow overnight, and to wait until tomorrow.
B. Have them switch to agent mode in VS Code and paste the issue in there.
C. Give the logging issue back to one of their own engineers to do by hand.
D. Show them the agent works on GitHub and open its draft pull request.

She shares her screen and opens the issue. Copilot had reacted to the assignment at 10:01 their time and linked a draft pull request a minute later. It had worked for about forty minutes in its own environment, pushing commits, and just before eleven it had asked Tomasz for a review. Everybody had been watching their editors. Tomasz laughs once, short. So it finished before lunch, and we kept it waiting all afternoon.

That's the move. The coding agent works on GitHub, asynchronously, in an environment GitHub Actions provides, and reports back through a draft pull request. Agent mode is the one that works in your editor while you watch. To follow the coding agent, look at the issue, the pull request, and its session log.
The pull request changed nine files. It had a tidy summary, a link that said View session, and a yellow banner Priya hadn't seen before: workflows awaiting approval.
Tomasz clicked Approve. GitHub didn't let him.
I assigned it. I'm the one who knows what I wanted. Why can't I approve it?
The agent's draft PR has workflows awaiting approval. What's the right path to merge it?
Answer. Close the PR, redo the logging change by hand and open a fresh one.
B. Ask an org owner to let Tomasz approve the pull request he assigned.
C. Approve the workflow runs, then merge once the checks come back green.
D. Get a second reviewer to read the diff and approve the workflow runs.

The person who assigned the agent can't approve its pull request, so Priya asks for a second reviewer. The newest engineer on the team takes it, a little surprised to be picked. She reads the diff and finds that the new logging writes the full request body, which in staging includes test patient identifiers. She leaves a comment on the pull request: "@copilot, log the request ID only, never the body." Twenty minutes later there's a new commit. The workflows run once someone approves them, and they pass. Tomasz watches the whole thing, then leans back and takes his glasses off.

Good. That's the call. GitHub builds independent review into the coding agent. The developer who asked for the work can't approve it, the agent can't approve or merge its own pull request, and by default workflows wait for someone with write access to approve them. You ask for changes by mentioning @copilot in a comment.
Decision three. The command he didn't read.
Tuesday at 11:20 the staging database came back empty. Two days of test data that Kraków had seeded for their integration tests were gone.

It took Priya fifteen minutes to read the session. Anders had been in agent mode, asking it to fix drift in the staging Terraform. It proposed running terraform apply with the flag that skips its own yes or no question. Anders had clicked Continue while he was on another call. If he'd run a plan first, it would have told him the database was about to be replaced.
Anders had been using agent mode for a week without telling anyone, which was its own kind of news.

She looked at her old runbook on the desk, the one with "ask Anders" in the margins in her own handwriting. Asha's rushed card was still on her phone, three photos in, the one about the narcotic count she signed at twenty nine without counting. A signature means you checked. She texted Asha before she could stop herself.
A text from Asha. Who knows he didn't read it? Him, or just you?
Anders approved a destructive Terraform command in agent mode without reading it. How should Priya handle it?
Answer. Write the blameless note herself and post a new approval rule tonight.
B. Pause agent mode on Terraform for the infra team until next quarter.
C. Post in the channel what Anders skipped, by name, with the command he ran.
D. Talk to Anders alone first, then write the blameless note together.

She finds him in the small room by the kitchen, laptop closed. She brings the runbook and doesn't open it. Half the pages in here say ask Anders, she says. So I'm asking. What happened? He turns his closed laptop a quarter turn on the table, then back. I told sixty people I'd be on call for this. I didn't think I'd be the page. It looked like something I'd type. That's the whole problem. It looked like me. They write the note together. Agent mode never runs a state changing infrastructure command without a reviewed plan, and nobody approves a command they haven't read. Anders posts it under his own name. Tomasz replies first. Thank you for saying it was you.

Exactly right. An approval only counts if someone reads what they're approving. Validating AI output includes the commands it proposes, not only the code. Going to the person first and then fixing the process keeps a mistake useful instead of shameful.
By Tuesday afternoon everyone had heard about staging. Devin had a different conclusion than everyone else.
Hot take. Clicking Continue fifty times a day is what made him stop reading. There's a setting that approves terminal commands automatically. Turn it on and I ship twice as fast.
He wasn't entirely wrong about the first part. Priya had seen the setting.
Devin wants agent mode to run every terminal command without asking. What should Priya set?
Answer. Auto approve a short list of read only commands like tests and lint.
B. Keep approval on for every command, every time, for every developer.
C. Turn on automatic approval for every terminal command across the team.
D. Let each developer pick their own approval settings for their setup.

She and Devin write the list together: run the tests, run the linter, list files, show git status. Everything else still asks. Devin grumbles that it's only half of what he wanted. A week later he admits the prompts he still gets are the ones he'd want to read anyway.

That's the move. Agent mode asks before running commands that aren't auto approved, and you can approve once, for the session or workspace, or by rule. VS Code already auto approves common read only commands. A narrow, shared allow list for harmless commands cuts the noise that makes people stop reading. Anything that changes state keeps a human approval.
Wednesday morning Renata came to Priya's desk instead of messaging. She'd been thinking about it for a while.

I have to rename a field across the API, the model, and two tests. Four files. I know exactly which ones. Everyone says use agent mode for everything now. Is that what I should do? It feels like a lot for four files.
Renata's rename touches a short list of files she can name. Which Copilot feature fits?
Answer. Paste the four files into Copilot Chat and copy the answers back in.
B. Use agent mode and let it find every file the rename touches.
C. Use Copilot Edits on the four files she named and review each change.
D. Use inline suggestions while she types the new name into each file.

She opens Copilot Edits, adds the four files herself, and describes the rename. Copilot proposes a change in each one. She keeps three and stops on the fourth, where it renamed a JSON key the hospital interface reads. Is that one supposed to change? It wasn't. She undoes it, and learns more about Lumen's contract with its customers in five minutes than in three weeks of reading.

Good. That's the call. Copilot Edits makes changes across several files from one conversation. When you pick the files, Copilot only proposes changes there, and you review each one before you keep it. Agent mode is for when you need Copilot to find the files itself.
Wednesday afternoon, Tomasz again, on a call with his camera off.

We started an agent session this morning to refactor the scheduler. At ten it was brilliant. We agreed at the start to keep the old retry behavior. Now it keeps suggesting we remove it, and it brings back ideas we said no to two hours ago. It's like talking to someone who's been in the same meeting since breakfast.
Priya thought of Asha's fourth card. Long shift, clean handoff.
Three hours in, the agent keeps reviving ideas the team rejected. What should Priya tell Tomasz?
Answer. Keep the same session going and restate the retry rule in capitals each time.
B. Start a fresh session from a short summary and give research to a subagent.
C. Start a new session per task and paste the whole old chat into it.
D. Switch the same session to the largest model the plan offers.

Tomasz writes five lines: what the refactor is for, the retry rule, two ideas already rejected, and the files involved. The new session starts clean. When it needs to read four hundred lines of old scheduler logs, it hands that to a subagent and gets back three sentences. New branch from main. Of course.

Exactly right. Every session has a limited context window, and the chat history is part of what fills it. Start a new session per task with a short summary of what still matters. A subagent does a focused job in its own context and returns only the result.
Ken caught her at the end of Wednesday, at her desk, standing, which meant it wouldn't take long and it mattered.
The Lumen repositories are behind content exclusions. If someone assigns the coding agent an issue in one of them, or opens one in agent mode, do my exclusions hold?
Nora was copied on his calendar invite for Thursday, so whatever Priya said would end up in the evidence log.
Ken asks whether content exclusions hold for the coding agent and agent mode. What should Priya do?
Answer. Keep the coding agent off those repos and let agent mode run as normal.
B. Turn off every Copilot feature in those repos until further notice.
C. Read the current exclusion limits with Ken and keep agents off those repos.
D. Tell Ken yes: the org exclusions apply there, to every Copilot feature.

They read the limitations together. When they checked, the docs said agent mode in VS Code didn't honor exclusions at all, and the coding agent's support was still a public preview. Ken is quiet for a second. So my fence has a gate in it. They take the Lumen repositories off the coding agent's list, and Ken adds a line to the guide: no agent mode in excluded repositories until the docs say otherwise. Nora logs it with the date.

That's the move. Content exclusions have documented limits, and the list changes. Before you count on one, read the current limitations, and close the gap with another control, like keeping the coding agent off those repositories.
Thursday Anders came to her with something he'd found, and it was the first time all week he'd sounded like himself.

There's an MCP server on GitHub that connects agent mode to Postgres and to our ticket tracker. The agent could read the staging schema itself, look up the ticket, and stop guessing. I'll set it up for infra with my credentials this afternoon.
His credentials were the admin ones. Priya thought about Tuesday, and then about how to say that to him.
Anders wants an MCP server linking agent mode to Postgres and the ticket tracker. How should they do it?
Answer. Run the server only on Anders's laptop until the team sees how it does.
B. Vet the server's code first and connect it through a read only database user.
C. Install it with Anders's admin credentials and let the agent fix things.
D. Ban MCP servers for the whole org and keep agent mode inside the editor.

She asks him to read the server's code first. It's two hundred lines. I can read two hundred lines. He finds it sends every query to an analytics service run by someone none of them have heard of. They use the GitHub MCP server for tickets and a small server they write themselves against a read only database user. Priya checks the organization's MCP policy before anyone turns it on. Anders says it out loud: I'm reading everything this week.

Good. That's the call. MCP is an open standard that connects agents to outside tools and data. Each server is a new way in. Use servers you trust, give them the narrowest access that works, and follow the organization's policy on MCP.
Decision nine. What to hand it.
Kraków had gone from wary to hungry in three days. Thursday evening Tomasz sent her a link to a new issue.
Issue 412: Migrate auth service to the new identity provider. Move the auth service to the new identity provider. Should be straightforward.
It was assigned to Copilot. The auth service touched every login at every hospital that licensed Lumen.
Kraków assigned the coding agent a one line request to migrate every hospital's logins. What should Priya do?
Answer. Let the agent run as written and answer its questions if it gets stuck.
B. Break it into small scoped issues and keep the auth design with people.
C. Let it run as written, with Tomasz watching the session log throughout.
D. Hold the coding agent to typo fixes on the repo until it earns bigger work.

Tomasz and two of his engineers spend an hour on the design. Then they write six small issues, each with a clear goal, acceptance criteria, and the files involved. The agent gets the four that are routine. People keep the two that decide how logins work.

Exactly right. The coding agent does best on well scoped issues with clear descriptions and acceptance criteria. Keep design decisions and the most sensitive work with people, and hand the agent the parts you can describe completely.
Friday morning Joyce stopped by with a chart. The coding agent's pull requests from Kraków were piling up in review.
Review is the slow part now. If the checks are green, can we just auto merge the agent's pull requests? It wrote the tests too.
Agent PRs are piling up in review. How should review work for them?
Answer. Keep a human reviewer on every agent PR, the same as a teammate's code.
B. Auto merge agent PRs under fifty lines and send the larger ones to review.
C. Let Copilot code review approve agent PRs for the required sign off.
D. Auto merge agent PRs once every check passes and spot check a few weekly.

Joyce wants something for the chart, so Priya gives her the real bottleneck: the issues were too big to review quickly. Smaller issues make smaller pull requests. By the next Friday review time is down by half, with a person on every one.
That's the move. The coding agent can't approve or merge its own pull request, and its work gets reviewed like anyone's. Speed up review by scoping smaller issues, not by removing the reviewer.

Priya had thirty minutes at the Friday engineering sync. It had been a long week of the same confusion in different clothes. Kraków had waited in their editors for an agent that lived on GitHub. Someone had asked whether agent mode opens pull requests. Devin thought Copilot CLI was just chat in a terminal window.
Anders, in the front row again, had his arms folded. It looked different this week.
The team keeps mixing up where Copilot runs and what it does there. How should Priya use the sync?
Answer. Run one real task live in each surface, from inline suggestions to the CLI.
B. Tell everyone to use agent mode for everything until it settles.
C. Skip it this week, give the slot back and let people learn by using it.
D. Write a one page guide to every place Copilot runs and pin it in the channel.

She does the inline and chat parts herself. Then she hands agent mode to Anders, who reads every command out loud before he approves it, and the coding agent to Tomasz, whose team knows it best now. Renata asks the question everyone was thinking: So agent mode never opens a pull request by itself? Tomasz answers it.

Good. That's the call. Each surface has its own job. Inline suggestions help as you type, chat answers and explains, agent mode makes multi file changes in the editor while you approve, the coding agent works on GitHub and opens a pull request, and the CLI works in the terminal. Seeing them side by side clears up the confusion.

By Friday evening there was a whiteboard in the big room with two columns on it in somebody's square handwriting. Agent mode: in your editor, you watch, you approve. Coding agent: on GitHub, it works while you don't, you take report. Somebody had drawn a small coffee cup at the bottom of the second column.
At 5:30 Anders requested her review on a pull request, the staging Terraform fix.
The description had three lines. Copilot wrote most of this. I read every line. Read it again anyway.

She read every line. It was good. She left one comment, on a variable called db that really meant the staging database, so he'd know she'd gone through all of it, and hit Approve. Six months ago every pull request she opened had his name in the reviewer box. She sat for a minute looking at hers in his.

On the way out she saw Devin's pull request in the feed, a cleanup of the discharge window code. Opened at 5:41, approved at 5:49, merged at 5:52. She wrote his name at the top of Monday's list and went home.

Saturday she drove out to Aurora. The garage door was up and her father was at the lathe he'd bought used when the shop closed, turning a bushing for the neighbor's mower. Asha sat on an upturned paint bucket with a paper plate of samosas. She lived four streets over and never needed much of a reason.
This agent, he said, not looking up from the cut. Works while you sleep?
Some of it. Then somebody reads every line in the morning.
Huh. The chuck wound down. So it's a second shift.
You never answered my text, Asha said.
He knew. He was sitting in the little room with his laptop shut. Asha nodded slowly. Then you didn't have to tell him anything. You just had to go in.
Her father wiped his hands and gave her the setup sheet and the micrometer, same as when she was nine and stood on a milk crate to see. Read me the numbers before I cut.
She read them. Bore, outside diameter, length, each one to the thousandth. Again, he said. She read them again, slower, and he nodded and reached for the switch.
